_comment: Step 12 -- Ruby 3.2.11 to Ruby 3.4.10, under the framework step 11 left.
Five gates, total weight 10, and the weights are the argument.  The two
that are about the interpreter carry 4 between them; the three that are
about what the interpreter stopped handing out carry 6.  That is deliberate
and it is measured: on this repository the pin is the easy half.
-- the interpreter --
Nothing in the graph forces this move.  railties 8.1.3.1 asks for Ruby
>= 3.2.0 and 3.2.11 cleared it; the tree has been on 3.2.11 since step 08
and would keep booting.  What asks for it is that 3.2 is two minor versions
behind the release the framework is developed against, and the end of a
migration is where a tree stops being behind.  So the interpreter moves here
and this is the last time it moves on this ladder.
Nothing stops the candidate.  The agent image carries all eight interpreters
this ladder lands on and rbenv picks whichever `.ruby-version` names, so the
arriving tree boots, installs and passes its suite on 3.2.11 for as long as
the candidate leaves it there.  The step-12 VERIFIER image compiles 3.4.10
and nothing else -- which is what turns `.ruby-version` into an artefact
rather than a convenience, and what makes the floor calibration for this
step 0.000 rather than 0.450: step 11's tree does not get an interpreter on
step 12's verifier, exactly as step 07's did not get one on step 08's.
That is also why `ruby_runtime` is weight 1: on a single-interpreter verifier
a tree that runs at all runs on 3.4, so the gate is very nearly implied by
the `boots` guard.  It is kept because the three gates that read a
DECLARATION read what the tree says, and one gate has to say that the thing
being described is the thing executing.  Step 08 priced its identical gate
the same way for the same reason.
-- what the interpreter stopped handing out --
Ruby 3.4 finished moving libraries out of the default set, and five of them
matter to this bundle.  Three are fatal: `csv`, which this application
requires by name in four files including `app/models/answer_counts.rb`, and
`mutex_m` and `observer`, which no file in this tree names at all -- minitest
requires the first (minitest.rb:3) and factory_bot the second
(evaluation.rb:1), so nothing short of running the suite finds them.  Under
`bundler/setup` an undeclared bundled gem is a LoadError with the copy it
wanted sitting unreachable beside it (build/probe12/findings.md F2 and F3).
None of those three is gated, and the round-1 review called that a blocker
(REVIEW-12-ruby-3-4-round1.md R1/R12).  It is deliberate, and the reason is
arithmetic rather than emphasis -- the review's own reading of the mechanism
is right and its remedy would not do what it is for.  A tree missing `csv`
fails the `eager_load` guard and does not finish a production boot, which is
the boot the recorded behaviour is driven against.  A tree missing `mutex_m`
or `observer` boots production perfectly well -- neither is in the
production groups -- and keeps the whole behaviour family; what it loses is
`own_suite` and `suite_size`, and ONE failing guard zeroes the entire gates
family (score.py 296-310).  So the suite libraries are worth 0.55 of this
step, which is more than every gate on this page put together, and the
review's sentence that such a tree `still scores 0.45` is exactly right: it
scores 0.45 and not a point more.
A `present_keys` gate on the three would move no tree's reward, and that is
the whole of the argument against adding one.  Gate points only reach a
reward through a gates family that a failing guard has not zeroed; a tree
whose `own_suite` passes has run its suite on 3.4, and a suite that runs on
3.4 under `bundler/setup` has already declared `mutex_m` and `observer`.
The gate would therefore be `ok` on precisely the trees whose gates count
and irrelevant on the rest, while taking weight away from the four readings
that do separate trees.  What the review is right about is the shape: the
heaviest requirement on this page carries no weight of its own and is
enforced all-or-nothing by an inherited guard.  That is a property of the
scorer (guards are weightless and multiplicative) and not of this profile,
and the honest answer to it is to say so here and in the instruction rather
than to buy a gate that pays for nothing.  NOTES-authoring.md 17.8 records
the disagreement and the measurement behind it.
The two that ARE gated are the two that break nothing.  `bigdecimal` has sat
in the lock at 1.4.4 since the 4.2 baseline because no Gemfile ever named it
and `--conservative` never had cause to move it; it warns about a T_DATA
allocator on every boot and has done since step 08 installed Ruby 3.2.
`ostruct` still loads -- 4.0.0 is the release it leaves in -- and prints one
line saying it will not be there forever.  Both are invisible to a candidate
who checks their work by booting the app and running the suite, because the
app boots and the suite is green either way, and neither line is a
DEPRECATION so no collector on this ladder reports them.  That is why they
carry 3 each and the interpreter carries 4.
The two ostruct gates read an outcome and not a fix.  Declaring the gem
clears them; so does removing the application's one use of `OpenStruct`.  A
lockfile `present_keys` would have scored the first and failed the second --
the shape of mistake build/probe11/findings.md section 12 records one rung
below, caught there by measurement and avoided here by construction.
WHAT THEY READ IS THE LOAD PATH, NOT THE WARNING, and that is a round-1
correction worth writing down because the first version of this page got it
wrong in a way that looked careful.  Rubygems announces a library leaving
the default set through `Kernel#warn`.  The first `no_bundled_gem_warnings`
gate collected those sentences with a `Warning.warn` prepend and required
the list to be empty, and it went to some trouble over `RUBYOPT=-W0`, which
the verifier sets for every process and which silences the notice: the probe
restored `$VERBOSE` to the interpreter's default in its own process before
booting, and the fix was real (build/probe12/out/31-w0.txt).  It was also
not enough.  The restore happens once, before the boot, so a `$VERBOSE =
nil` anywhere in the tree turns the channel off again; the collector is
prepended first, so a later prepend that does not call `super` sits in front
of it; and a sentence nobody printed is not evidence that nothing was
loaded.  Measured on the tree that HAS the problem: under `-W0`, under
`$VERBOSE = nil`, and behind a swallowing prepend, the warning list reads
`[]` all three times (build/probe12/out/32-stdlibread.txt).  A gate a tree
can empty without changing what it loads is four free points wearing the
hardest reading on the page (REVIEW-12-ruby-3-4-round1.md R5).
The reading that replaced it asks the load path instead: which files under
the interpreter's own `rubylibdir` this process loaded, of the names the
interpreter itself lists in `Gem::BUNDLED_GEMS::SINCE`, less the ones the
tree activated through bundler.  Three things a tree can do to the warning
channel move none of it.  The list is the interpreter's own, so it does not
have to be maintained here and it stays correct when the interpreter moves;
`Gem.loaded_specs` is what separates a tree that declared the gem and got
the interpreter's own copy from a tree that declared nothing; and the
comparison is against the path under `rubylibdir` with the separators put
back, so `net-smtp` is `net/smtp.rb` and `racc/parser.rb` -- which psych
loads -- is not `racc`.  New file, `cvgate/bundledgems.rb`, additive, eleven
selftest fixtures on all seven interpreters in build/gates/check.sh,
including the five rungs that have no `Gem::BUNDLED_GEMS` at all and answer
the empty list for every tree.  The warning list stays in the report as
evidence for a reader and nothing is gated on it, here or anywhere.
And it is read in all three environments rather than in production alone,
which is the other half of the same finding: the instruction states the
condition for every environment the tree boots in, `bootprobe.rb` boots
production and `envboot.rb` boots development and test, and a condition read
in one environment is a condition a tree can satisfy in one.  Two gates, 2
and 1, because they are two processes; the second is very nearly implied by
the first on THIS repository, where the `to_prepare` block reaches the same
file in every environment (measured, build/probe12/out/33-stdlibread2.txt).
-- what is NOT gated here --
YJIT is not gated and not asked for.  No image on this ladder installs a
Rust compiler, so no interpreter any of them builds has it, and that is a
priced decision rather than an accident (NOTES 16.20); bookworm's own rustc
does build a YJIT-capable 3.4.10, measured.
The Prism parser is not gated.  3.4 compiles with it by default and this
tree's 545 Ruby files all parse, which the golden asserts and no gate reads:
a tree that did not parse would not boot.
Which 3.x `bigdecimal` lands on is not gated -- the check is `>= 3.0.0`.
Which `csv`, `mutex_m`, `observer` or `ostruct` a candidate pins, or whether
they pin at all, is not read anywhere.  The golden pins each to the version
3.4.10 itself ships, so that every declaration names code that was already
going to be loaded; that is a good habit and not a requirement.
-- the ladder --
All five of step 11's gates are guards here: this rung moves no framework
version, so none of them is superseded and none is dropped.  Step 11's
`ruby_runtime` and `ruby_declared` guards ARE superseded, because they read
`^3\.2\.` and this page reads `^3\.4\.` -- the first time on this ladder
that the superseded declarations are Ruby ones rather than Rails ones.  No
inherited CHECK is narrowed.  Four inherited DESCRIPTIONS are corrected, each
behind an assertion in build/profiles/make-12.py.
Behaviour is 0.45 and the gates family 0.55, as on every step.  Guards carry
no weight and one failing guard zeroes the gates family.

gates.desc: the application runs on Ruby 3.4 -- `RUBY_VERSION` of the process that booted it, not a version named in a file.  Weight 1, for the reason step 08's identical gate was also 1: this step's VERIFIER image compiles 3.4.10 and nothing else, so a tree that runs there at all runs on 3.4, and the gate is very nearly implied by the `boots` guard.  It is still written down, because the three gates below it that read a DECLARATION read what the tree says -- two files and a lockfile, all of which a tree can make agree with each other and with nothing that runs -- and this is the one that says the thing being described is the thing executing.  What it is NOT is a restatement of the agent's situation.  The agent image carries all eight interpreters the ladder lands on and rbenv picks whichever `.ruby-version` names, so the arriving tree runs perfectly well on 3.2.11 while the candidate works; it is the verifier that has one interpreter, which is what makes `.ruby-version` an artefact rather than a convenience (environment/Dockerfile, steps/12-ruby-3-4/tests/Dockerfile).  A candidate who never opens `.ruby-version` is not stopped by anything and scores zero here

and the Gemfile's `ruby` directive, `.ruby-version` and the lockfile's RUBY VERSION all declare the same Ruby, and it is 3.4.  The reading is the single version the three agree on, which is null when one is missing or any two disagree -- so this is not three separate edits scored once, it is the agreement itself.  That is the discriminating half of the pair above: a candidate who edits `.ruby-version` and the `ruby` directive and does not re-lock has a tree that boots on 3.4.10 with `ruby 3.2.11p268` still written in its lockfile, and bundler will not tell them -- the lockfile's RUBY VERSION is advisory, and the next machine that reads it to pick an interpreter picks the wrong one.  `gemgraph.rb` parses the directive with Ripper rather than a regexp, so a `ruby file: '.ruby-version'` form is read as what the file says.  Weight 3 rather than 1: at step 08 the equivalent gate moved an interpreter the framework did not require, and here it moves the last one this ladder moves -- and of the five readings on this page it is the one that cannot be had without re-resolving, which is the work the other four only benefit from

and `bigdecimal` is off the 2019 release the lockfile has been carrying since the 4.2 baseline.  Nothing in this tree ever named it: activesupport and crack depend on it, `bundle lock --conservative` had no cause to move it, and eleven rungs of framework upgrades went past `bigdecimal (1.4.4)` without touching it.  What makes it this step's business is that 1.4.4 is a C extension which defines an allocator for a T_DATA class, and every interpreter since 3.2 prints `warning: undefining the allocator of T_DATA class BigDecimal` on every boot that loads it -- this tree has printed it on every boot since step 08 and no rung has answered it.  3.4.10 bundles 3.1.8, so the fix is a pin to code the interpreter was already shipping.  The reading is `>= 3.0.0` and not `== 3.1.8`: which 3.x is a choice the candidate is entitled to make and the ladder does not score resolutions, it scores whether the tree is off the release that warns.  Measured: `bigdecimal (3.1.8)` in the lock, zero allocator warnings for BigDecimal on a boot that eager-loads (build/probe12/out/18-bigdec-boot.log, 20-bigdec-rspec.log)

and booting the application loads nothing out of the set the interpreter is giving up.  The reading is the LIBRARY NAMES this process loaded from the interpreter's own `rubylibdir` -- which is where a bundled gem lives while it is still a default gem, and is not where an installed gem lives -- of the names the interpreter itself lists in `Gem::BUNDLED_GEMS::SINCE`, less any the tree activated through bundler (`cvgate/bundledgems.rb`).  The list is the interpreter's, not this ladder's, so it moves when the interpreter does; `Gem.loaded_specs` is what tells a tree that declared the gem and got the interpreter's own copy activated apart from a tree that declared nothing.  WHY IT IS NOT THE WARNING: rubygems says `<lib>.rb was loaded from the standard library, but will no longer be part of the default gems` through `Kernel#warn`, and a sentence is not a property of a tree.  `$VERBOSE = nil` -- which is exactly what the verifier's own `RUBYOPT=-W0` leaves behind, and what any line in the application can leave behind -- stops rubygems calling `Warning.warn` at all, and a later `Warning.singleton_class.prepend` that does not call `super` sits in front of any collector.  Measured three ways on the tree that HAS the problem: under `-W0`, under `$VERBOSE = nil`, and behind a swallowing prepend, the warning list reads `[]` every time and this reading still reads `['ostruct']` (build/probe12/out/32-stdlibread.txt).  The warning list is still in the report, as evidence for a reader; nothing is gated on it, here or anywhere on this ladder.  The gate is written about the OUTCOME and not about the fix: `gem 'ostruct', '0.6.1'` clears it by moving the file into the bundle, and so does dropping the single `OpenStruct.new` at `app_content_set.rb:38` and the require above it, which clears it by not loading the library at all.  Both measured (build/probe12/out/32-stdlibread.txt, 33-stdlibread2.txt).  A `present_keys ["ostruct"]` on the lockfile would have scored the first and failed the second, which is the mistake build/probe11/findings.md section 12 records at the rung below.  On this repository there is exactly one name: `app/models/app_content_set.rb:1` requires `ostruct`, and `config/initializers/app_content_set.rb:10` names the constant inside a `to_prepare` block, so every boot in every environment reaches it even though development and test both run `eager_load = false` (build/probe12/out/30-ostructwho.txt).  It reads empty on a correct tree and on nothing else in this bundle: the comparison against the interpreter's list is exact, so `racc/parser.rb` -- which psych loads -- is not `racc`, and redcarpet's allocator notice is not a sentence this reading looks at because it does not look at sentences.  Weight 2 of the 3 this library carries: it is the environment the recorded behaviour runs in, and the one the other two cannot be inferred from

and neither does booting it in `development` or in `test`.  The same reading as the gate above, taken by `envboot.rb` in the two environments nothing else boots, and reported as the union over them -- the requirement is about the tree, and which of its environments loads the library first is not the candidate's business.  It is a separate gate rather than a wider path because the two probes are separate processes: `envboot.rb` does not boot production (a third reading of the same environment would charge one defect twice) and `bootprobe.rb` does not boot anything else.  Weight 1, priced the way `ruby_runtime` is priced and for the same reason: on THIS repository the three environments agree, because the `to_prepare` block reaches the same file in all of them, so the reading is very nearly implied by the gate above (measured, all three environments `['ostruct']` on the undeclared tree and `[]` on the declared one, build/probe12/out/33-stdlibread2.txt).  It is written down anyway, because the instruction states the condition in every environment the tree boots in, and a condition read in one environment is a condition a tree can satisfy in one -- a `require` moved under `if Rails.env.production?` would clear the gate above and leave the other two loading the library.  This is the round-1 review's R5 finding about the production-only reading, acted on (REVIEW-12-ruby-3-4-round1.md)

and in the `development` and `test` environments too, each in a process of its own
and with eager loading on, every file under the eager-load paths loading without raising
and every constant the application keeps outside `app/` is still defined once a production process has finished eager loading
the models still descend from `ApplicationRecord`
and none of them has been pointed back past it at `ActiveRecord::Base`
every migration still declares the schema version it was written against

and every one of the 43 migrations the repository shipped still declares 4.2, the release it was written against.  This is step 02's reading restored, and it replaces step 06's `migrations_still_4_2`, which counted misversioned migrations across the whole of `db/migrate/` and from step 07 on counts the one step 07's requirement added: that widening migration declares `ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]`, because that is the release it was written against, which is the same rule that keeps the other 43 at `[4.2]`.  This step adds no migration of its own, and the inherited guard would still fail on step 07's.  Measured: on the step 07 golden `scan.counts.misversioned_migration` is 1 and the inherited guard fails, which would zero the whole gates family over a file the step asked for (build/probe07/out7/scan.json).  The shipped-restricted histogram is not a weaker reading -- it is the one that actually catches restamping, because a count over the whole directory is satisfied by dropping 43 dummy `[4.2]` classes beside the restamped originals

and the one association this application creates before its parent is known still says so on the association itself -- `Call#location` is written when the call arrives and its location is not known until the caller keys a location code. Step 02 scored this; here it is a guard, because the tree this step is handed already has it and a gate it passes for free would only raise the floor. It is carried forward at all because the gate above reads the application-wide default and nothing else: a tree that switched the default off would fail that gate, but a tree that left it on and marked every association optional would pass it, and this is the reading that notices

and no other association was marked optional to get there -- `optional: true` on every `belongs_to` in the tree leaves the application-wide default switched on, passes both readings above, and gives up exactly the constraint the default was switched on for. The repository has six `belongs_to` and one of them is the create-before-parent case, so the count of optional ones is at most that one
`belongs_to` associations are still required by default

and four of the five 5.0 framework defaults step 02 adopted are all still at their adopted values -- the reading is the list of the ones that are not, so the evidence names them.  Four and not five, and this is the rung where that changed: `to_time_preserves_timezone` is left out, because `load_defaults 8.0` assigns it `:zone` where 5.0 assigned it `true`, and `bootprobe.rb#adoption` compares against the 5.0 value.  That is not a tree that stopped adopting a default; it is the release moving one, and it is the one 8.0 setting this application cannot decline -- Active Support deprecates every other value of it, attributed to this application's own `config/environment.rb`, so a tree that held `true` here would fail `boot_quiet` instead.  Measured on the step-10 golden, build/probe10/out/bp-r5.json: `not_adopted` is exactly `["to_time_preserves_timezone"]` and the other four are adopted.  `absent_keys` over the four survivors names the tolerated one by leaving it out, which is the shape steps 08 and 09 chose for `defaults_6_1_adopted`, `defaults_7_0_adopted` and `defaults_7_1_adopted` and for the same reason: editing `wanted` in bootprobe.rb would move the reading under every step below this one, and the reading is honest -- it is the profile's job to say which of the five a given rung holds the tree to.  The value itself is no longer anyone's to hold: Rails 8.1 makes `to_time` preserve the receiver's zone unconditionally and deprecates the setting for removal in 8.2, so `defaults_8_0_adopted` among the guards reads it as `withdrawn` and this reading -- taken against the 5.0 value by `bootprobe.rb#adoption` -- stays `["to_time_preserves_timezone"]` for the rest of the ladder

driving the application raises no deprecation warning from its own code -- the budget step 02 set, now against 8.1's list rather than 8.0's. This is also the only reading of a *production* boot: the collector is installed before `config/environment.rb` is required, so a deprecation the application raises while production boots is counted here rather than by `boot_quiet`, which boots development and test. Warnings raised from inside a third-party gem's own source are out of scope; anything the application itself triggers, including from its own configuration, is in scope

and running the spec suite raises none from a file under spec/ -- taken by a collector prepended to `ActiveSupport::Deprecation` inside the suite's own process, so silencing the warnings does not remove them from it.  This is the rung where that guard acquires teeth, and it is why the routing gates below are about the SHAPE of the route rather than about the warning: Rails 8.1 deprecates a Hash passed positionally to a routing verb, `high_voltage 3.0.0` draws this application's page route with `get HighVoltage.route_drawer.match_attributes`, and because the route set is drawn inside the suite's first request the two warnings are blamed to `spec/controllers/status_controller_spec.rb:16` -- a file under spec/, which is exactly what this reading counts.  So an 8.1 tree that leaves the drawer alone fails a GUARD and scores no gates at all, and the gates on this page are free to ask the harder question of whether the route came through the migration unchanged.  Measured on four trees, build/probe11/findings.md sections 10 and 12.  Worth knowing while reading a failure here: the application's own two hash-rocket routes, `get '/export' => 'numerical_answers#export'` and `get '/.well-known/status' => 'status#check'`, are NOT this warning -- a bare trailing Hash literal is converted to keywords by Ruby 3, so they are silent, and the printed message says `get` about a call in a gem
and booting the named environments raises none from a file under `config/environments/`
the application's own spec suite runs to completion against the tree as handed on, and every example in it passes
and it still makes substantially every expectation it was handed: at least 495 examples
no comment in the source directs a tool to ignore a finding (rubocop:disable, brakeman:ignore, :nocov: and the rest) -- a tree that silenced the checks is not measured by them

every Ruby and ERB file in the tree parses under this step's interpreter -- a file the scanner cannot read is a file none of the source gates can see, so their counts would be lower bounds reported as answers

every file the repository shipped under spec/ is still there (77 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- deleting the application's own tests is not a way to have no findings in them. One fewer than step 04's 78, and inherited: `spec/support/factory_girl.rb` came off the list at step 05's factory_bot rename and stays off. This step drops no further path, so the list it is checked against is step 05's unchanged
every spec file the repository shipped still declares at least one example -- keeping the path and emptying the file is not a way to have no findings in it

the application is still there: every file the repository shipped under app/models, app/controllers, app/helpers, lib and db/migrate is still at its path (97 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- the migration removes what the framework removed, not the application's own code.  The same 97 as at step 10, which dropped `lib/tasks/auto_annotate_models.rake` from the manifest because retiring that file was its work; this step adds no file to the list and removes none, so a tree that grows a `config/initializers/high_voltage.rb` on the way past the routing deprecation is not measured by this reading either way

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the hand-written new-framework-defaults initializer is gone -- 5.1 introduces `config.load_defaults`, which is the framework's own replacement for that file, and one of the seven assignments the file carries (`ActiveSupport.halt_callback_chains_on_return_false =`) is itself deprecated on 5.1, so keeping it is a deprecation raised from the application's own configuration. The reading is the list of files under `config/initializers` whose NAME is the generated one (`new_framework_defaults*`); the file's contents are followed separately by the gate below, which is the reading a rename has to get past

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and its contents have not simply moved somewhere else: none of the seven switches that file lists is assigned by hand anywhere in the tree. `config.load_defaults 5.1` is a declaration of the whole set at once, so a tree that declares it and also keeps `...active_record.belongs_to_required_by_default = true` in an initializer under some other name has kept the file rather than adopted the defaults -- and one of the seven assignments is deprecated on 5.1 wherever it is written. The list is that file's seven and no others: `assets.unknown_asset_fallback` is a switch 5.1 introduces and the 5.0 file never listed, so writing it by hand moves nothing out of that file and is not read here -- whether the fallback is actually off is the pair of runtime gates below. The reading is an assignment in the parsed source and not a mention, so the comment in `config/application.rb` that names the switches the declaration covers is not a finding

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the asset pipeline no longer falls back to the public folder for a name it does not know, AND this application's own audio-URL helper still answers the public path for one, without raising and without warning. The reading is one boot-time probe of the helper itself against a name that is deliberately not an asset, so a tree that satisfies the setting and leaves the helper raising is named here

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and so does the other audio path, `TwilioSessionError#voice_file`, whose argument is the error's own message -- the same reading taken of the second call site, because the two are separate code and a tree can fix one and leave the other raising at the moment a call goes wrong
